cupidity

kyoo-PID-i-tee · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Cupidity is an excessive, often shameful desire for wealth or possessions.

The board members later admitted that cupidity, not the good of the shareholders, had guided most of their decisions that year.

Example

Historians describe the conquistador's cupidity for gold as the true engine behind the expedition, far more than any wish to spread the faith.

Cupidity isn't ordinary wanting -- it's an excessive, often corrupting greed for wealth or possessions.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

greed: Greed is the broad, everyday word for wanting more than you need -- more food, more money, more attention. Cupidity is narrower and harsher: an excessive, shameful craving aimed at wealth and possessions in particular, the kind of wanting that corrupts a person's judgment.

covetousness: Covetousness is longing for what belongs to someone else -- a neighbor's new car, a rival's trophy. Cupidity does not care who owns a thing: it is an excessive craving for wealth and possessions in general. Covetousness eyes your treasure; cupidity just wants treasure.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

generosity: a willingness to give freely

altruism: selfless concern for the well-being of others

Where it sits · how greedy the wanting becomes

desire → cupidity → avarice

desire vs. cupidity: Desire is a normal, ordinary wish for something, without the shameful excess of cupidity.

avarice vs. cupidity: Avarice is an even more extreme, all-consuming greed than ordinary cupidity -- miserly, hoarding, and always about wealth.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — cupid-: desire, longing (Latin cupere, 'to desire')

suffix — -ity: state of, quality of (Latin/French)

Put it together: Cupidity comes from Latin cupiditas, from cupere ('to desire') -- the same root behind the name Cupid, the Roman god of desire. Add -ity ('state of') and you get 'the state of desiring,' taken to a greedy extreme.

Use the root in a new word: Cupid: In Roman mythology, Cupid's name comes straight from the Latin verb cupere. Painters show him as a mischievous winged boy with a bow and arrows, hovering on clouds and choosing his targets with care.

Word Building

Word Choice

Cupidity always carries a disapproving tone -- it names greed strong enough to corrupt someone's judgment or morals, not simple everyday wanting.
